p: Three weeks have gone by since the last chapter.
In the week before Thanksgiving, Ken switched on Copilot CLI, and Anders made it explain the staging module he wrote in 2019.
Devin wanted a nightly job that would fix staging with every approval turned off. It became a script that only reports, and Anders wrote the rule: no allow all in any scheduled job.
Priya checked a list of twenty eight unused seats by hand, and twenty came off before the December bill.
Anders's guide to Copilot CLI went out after Priya reviewed it, and she added her own line at the bottom: if it looks wrong, stop it and call.
It's the middle of December now, and the quarter ends with the month.
Elena Vasquez. Halcyon's founder. She gave Priya this job.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer, now on infra. Her first big pull request is this week.
Tomasz Nowak. Leads Kraków. Most mornings, the first call.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Lately he volunteers for things.
Nora Kim. Compliance. The auditors come in March.
Ken Ito. Security lead. Still careful, still brief.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. He used to review Priya's work. Lately she reviews his.
Elena's email came at 6:12 on a Monday morning, ten weeks to the minute after the first one. This time Priya was already up, dressed, with her own list half written.

An email from Elena Vasquez. Subject: Thursday. Priya, The board meets Thursday at ten. They'll ask me whether Copilot was worth it. I'd like them to hear it from you. Yes or no first, then whatever you need to say. Elena
It was the first email Elena had ever sent to her alone. She read it twice anyway.

Asha's cards came at 6:30, five photos, purple felt tip. On the back of the last one: No more after these. You know where I am. Across the top card: Week eleven. Report. Tell me what you'd tell the next shift.
At 6:50, Joyce. Elena told me she wrote you. I'll be in the room Thursday. It's your answer.
She drove in with the radio off, making the list she'd been putting off since Thanksgiving. What had worked. What hadn't. What she still didn't know, which was the longest part.
Asha's first card said: Report is what happened on your shift. Not what you hoped happened. The next nurse needs the real one.

Under it Priya wrote what the GitHub docs say. Copilot usage metrics show how people adopt and use Copilot: daily and weekly active users, chat requests by mode, agent use, acceptance rate, lines of code suggested and added, and pull request activity such as merges and median time to merge. They come as dashboards at the enterprise and organization level, and as REST API reports for an enterprise or organization, including per repository and per user reports. The Copilot usage metrics policy has to be on. Then an organization owner, or someone given a custom role that can view the organization's Copilot metrics, can call GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/metrics/reports/organization-28-day/latest, which returns signed links to the last 28 days.

Know what the report can't see. Most of it comes from IDE telemetry. People with telemetry off can still count as active through server side signals, but their breakdowns by feature and their lines of code stay empty. Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and GitHub Mobile aren't included, and the data runs two to three days behind. Seat and license questions go to the user management API from last chapter. GitHub's advice is to read the signals together and add what people say in surveys and retros. Lines of code are a directional view of output, not value. A high acceptance rate means suggestions are relevant and trusted. It doesn't mean they're right.

How the exam asks it. Usage and engagement come from the usage metrics dashboards and API, with the metrics policy on. Seats come from the user management API. Settings changes come from the audit log.
The second card: An old chart is still the patient's chart. Read all of it before you rewrite the orders.

Copilot helps most with the legacy work people put off. It can explain code nobody remembers, add comments and documentation (/explain, and /doc in some editors), and translate between languages. GitHub's cookbook turns a Perl script into TypeScript with a prompt that asks for exactly the same behavior and output. Two warnings come with that. Copilot Chat's responses are non deterministic, so the same prompt can give different code. And a translation that compiles can still behave differently. The safe order is to explain the old code, write tests that pin what it does today, convert it in small pieces, and compare old and new outputs on the same input.

Day to day, three jobs come up over and over: writing new code, refactoring, and documenting. Here are all three on one small job, a nightly script that loops over hospitals. New code: ask Chat for a TypeScript function that processes a list in batches, and name the input, the batch size, and what it should log. Refactoring: select a tangled block, ask Copilot to refactor it into a small named function with no change in behavior, and run the pinned tests to show nothing moved. Documentation: ask for doc comments on each exported function and a short README section, then cut any sentence that claims something the code doesn't do. Now try the same three moves on something different. Take a fifty line shell script nobody owns. Ask Copilot to explain the code, then refactor it into named functions, then write a usage comment at the top. The trap is treating a refactor like a rewrite. A refactor keeps the behavior the same, and the tests are how you know it did.

Tests need data. Copilot can generate sample data and mock objects, so tests don't depend on real services or real people. Start with the goal, then list the specific requirements. Give context, such as the schema or types file. Name each edge case you need, because "realistic" leaves Copilot guessing. Then show an example. One is one-shot, several is few-shot. Examples teach shape fast. Ask for invented data, and read it before you use it. If the real data sits behind a content exclusion, leave the exclusion alone. An example you write by hand is the fix.
How the exam asks it. Legacy code: explain, test, convert in steps, compare. Sample data: goal, specifics, schema as context, named edge cases, an invented example. Never real rows.
The third card: We all learned on mannequins. Nobody ever charted one as a patient.

A unit test checks one piece alone. Mocks stand in for the database and other services, so it runs fast and the same way every time. An integration test checks that pieces work together, such as the new code against a test database or a real command. GitHub's own example still mocks the outside service and checks that your code calls it the right way, so using a mock doesn't make a test a unit test. With the code selected, /tests generates unit tests, and GitHub says they may not cover every scenario, so read them and add what's missing. A test prompt should name the edge cases, the errors you expect, and the inputs to reject, and each test should assert something specific. Open an existing test file in a tab, and Copilot follows your framework.

Copilot Chat can look for common vulnerabilities, like injection and cross site scripting, and suggest fixes such as parameterized queries, input validation, and passing arguments instead of building command strings. GitHub says plainly not to rely on it for a comprehensive security analysis. Code scanning does that job. It can also find performance hotspots: slow loops, repeated work, things that could be cached or run in parallel. Treat a performance suggestion as a change to measure, not a finding. Making one part faster can overload the part behind it.
How the exam asks it. Mocks isolate unit tests; integration tests check the pieces together. Copilot's security help is real but not comprehensive, so keep code scanning. Measure performance changes.
The fourth card: A drawing of a wound can teach you a lot. You still don't chart from it.

On GitHub, a pull request's description box, or a comment box, has a Copilot icon in its header, with Summary under it. It doesn't take existing text in the description into account, so start with a blank one. Then review it. A summary describes the diff. It can't know why you made the change, how you tested it, or what you're unsure of, and it can be wrong about behavior. Add those yourself. A summary also doesn't update when you push more commits, and a commit message Copilot writes in GitHub Desktop or on GitHub.com only covers the changes that were there when you asked. When the work changes, generate a new one and read it again.

The exam outline lists GitHub Spark, so know what it was. Spark opened in public preview in July 2025 for Copilot Pro+, reached Copilot Enterprise that fall, and built full stack apps from a plain language description, with hosting and AI features included, though AI features that called GitHub Models stopped on July 30, 2026. On August 4, 2026, GitHub stopped taking new Spark users and new apps. Existing users could export until August 31, and deployed apps keep running. Whatever you build a prototype with, its sample data is a design aid. Presenting it as results misleads people, and that's what transparency, one of the responsible AI principles GitHub follows, is about.
How the exam asks it. Start a pull request summary from a blank description and review it. Spark built apps from natural language and, as of October 2026, is retired. A prototype isn't evidence.
The last card: Two nurses sign the narcotic count. The cabinet counts too. It doesn't sign.

By default Copilot code review leaves a Comment review, never Approve or Request changes, so it doesn't count toward required approvals. Every review has an approval assessment in its overview comment, Copilot's view of whether the pull request is ready, and on its own that doesn't count either. Copilot approvals, in public preview as of October 2026, are off by default. Enterprise, organization, and repository settings can let Copilot approve and let those approvals count toward merge requirements, and a repository can limit that to pull requests where every changed file matches one of up to 15 file globs. Automatic reviews can be set by a user for their own pull requests, or by a repository admin, or by an organization or enterprise owner, through rulesets. So read what a question tells you about the setup. Where it happens: approvals that count live on pull requests on GitHub.com, under branch rules. What the plan and policies allow: the organization's Copilot plan and its owners' policies decide whether the feature is there at all. What's switched on: if nobody turned on Copilot approvals, Copilot's review is a comment and doesn't count. If an admin turned them on and every changed file matches the allowed paths, it can count. Preview features change, so know how it works now, not how it worked when the outline was written.

GitHub says Copilot isn't guaranteed to catch every problem and tells you to back it with human review. The cloud agent can't approve its own pull requests, and the person who asked for its work can't approve that work either. Accountability stays with people. Transparency means reporting what worked, what broke, what it cost, and what you don't know yet.

How the exam asks it. By default Copilot code review leaves Comment reviews that don't count toward required approvals. Copilot approvals are in preview and off by default. Where the plan and policies allow it and an admin turns them on, they can count, limited by path. Answer from the setup the question gives and from current behavior.
At 7:40 Tomasz called with his camera on. It was 3:40 in the afternoon in Kraków, and he had the oldest ticket in Halcyon's backlog open on his screen.

Retire run_forecasts.pl. Elena wrote it in 2016, before Halcyon had an office. Every night it starts the forecasts, one hospital unit at a time. Since 2019 people only add hospitals to it. My team says Copilot can turn it into TypeScript by Friday.
Renata was on the call too. She'd joined the infra rotation on December 1, and this was her first ticket on it.
Nobody here reads Perl. That's the problem. It's also why they want to hand it to Copilot.
Kraków wants Copilot to turn Elena's 2016 Perl script into TypeScript by Friday. How should Renata approach it?
A. Have Copilot translate the whole script at once and ship it when it compiles.
B. Have Copilot explain it, pin that with tests, then convert it in small pieces.
C. Leave the script in Perl and keep adding hospitals to it by hand.
D. Translate it in one pass with Copilot, then review the full diff line by line.

Kraków asks Copilot Chat to explain the script one section at a time. It reads every hospital config, loops through the units, starts the forecast command for each one, and writes a status file. The explanation turns up something nobody knew: units marked paused get skipped, a rule Elena added in 2018 for a hospital that closed a wing. That goes into the tests first. Then they convert it in four pieces, and staging runs old and new side by side every night to compare. Friday was optimistic. Friday was a guess.

That's the one I'd sign. Copilot is good at explaining legacy code and translating it to another language. But its answers vary from run to run, and a translation that compiles can still behave differently. Explain it first, pin today's behavior with tests, convert in small pieces, and compare the outputs.
Decision two. Where the numbers live.
At ten Joyce and Nora came to her desk together, which usually meant one of them had a question and the other had a deadline.
Elena wants numbers Thursday. Not stories. How many people use it, how they use it, and whether anything got faster.
And where each number came from, so I can find it again in March.

Halcyon was one organization on the Team plan, with no enterprise account above it. Ken had turned on the Copilot usage metrics policy in October, the week Nora first asked for numbers. Joyce had pulled a count from it for Finance in October and again in November, and read the first line both times. Nobody had downloaded the full report.
Elena wants adoption numbers by Thursday, each with a findable source. Where should they come from?
A. Download the org's 28 day usage metrics report and cite the API call.
B. Use November's seat census, with each person's last activity date.
C. Ask Copilot Chat on GitHub.com how much Halcyon's engineers have used it.
D. Count each person's events in the audit log, filtered to action:copilot.

Priya pulls the organization's latest twenty eight day report from the metrics API. It comes back as links to files, and the files hold the last 28 days: daily and weekly active users, chat by mode, agent use, acceptance rate, lines suggested and added, pull request counts, and merge times. Nora reads the fine print with her. Most of it comes from editor telemetry, so people with telemetry off count as active but show no detail. Chat on GitHub.com and mobile aren't in it. It runs two to three days behind. So it's what people did in their editors, a few days ago. That's the honest version.

That's how I'd chart it. Copilot usage metrics come as dashboards and REST API reports. With the usage metrics policy on, an organization owner, or someone with a custom role that can view its Copilot metrics, can download the org's latest 28 day report from the REST API's Copilot metrics reports endpoint. Most data is IDE telemetry; GitHub.com chat and mobile aren't included.
Decision three. Hospitals that don't exist.
Tuesday at nine Renata needed hospitals.
The tests for the new scheduler had to read hospital configs. The real ones lived under config/hospitals, behind Ken's exclusion since October. Copilot couldn't see them, which was the point.

Her first prompt had been one line: make some hospital configs for testing. Copilot gave her three. They were tidy and the same shape. None had a paused unit, a unit with no beds, or a name with anything in it but letters.
How do I get it to make the weird ones?
A. Attach the types file and list each odd case with one made up example.
B. Paste one real hospital's config into the chat, renamed, as the example.
C. Ask again and add that the configs should be realistic with edge cases.
D. Lift the exclusion on one hospital's config for an hour to show Copilot.

She attaches the config types file, which isn't excluded, and writes the goal first: twelve test hospitals for the scheduler, all invented. Then the specifics, one per line: a paused unit, a unit with zero beds, a hospital with forty units, a unit name with an apostrophe and a number in it. Under that she types one example config by hand, for a hospital that doesn't exist. What comes back has every edge she asked for. One made up name sounds too close to a real hospital, so she changes it. Larkin's 4 West stays. I gave it one example and it got the shape. That's one shot. Give it three and it's few shot.

That's what I'd want on my shift. Start with the goal, then list specific requirements. Give context, like a schema or types file, and an example of what you want: one example is one shot, several is few shot. Ask for invented data and read it before you use it. The exclusion stays.
Tuesday at two Renata's tests were green. All twenty six. By then her test hospitals had every odd case she could think of in them, down to a unit called Larkin's 4 West.

She'd selected the new scheduler and run /tests, with one of Kraków's test files open in the next tab so Copilot would match their framework. The tests mocked the forecast command and the database, so they ran in four seconds.
Tomasz read them on his phone, on a tram. Very green. Has it started a forecast yet?
It hadn't. Nothing in the tests had started anything.
Twenty six unit tests pass in four seconds with everything mocked. What should Renata do next?
A. Merge it, with twenty six passing tests covering every function in the file.
B. Run the new scheduler by hand in staging tonight and watch what it does.
C. Take the mocks out and point the same unit tests at the real services.
D. Keep them and add integration tests that run the real forecast command.

She keeps the unit tests and asks Copilot for integration tests: start the scheduler against a test database seeded with her test hospitals, and call the real forecast command in its dry run mode. The first one fails at 3:10. The scheduler builds the forecast command as one string, and Larkin's 4 West breaks it at the apostrophe. The mock never cared what the string looked like. That's why we have both.

That's the one I'd sign. Unit tests check one piece alone, with mocks standing in for databases and services, so they're fast. Integration tests check that the pieces work together. Copilot can write both, and /tests may not cover every scenario, so review them and add the edges.
By Wednesday morning the integration test that failed at 3:10 was the most read file in Kraków.
At eight Renata selected the scheduler and asked Copilot Chat to look for security problems and anything slow.

A message from Copilot Chat. 1. The forecast command is built as one string from config values, then run through a shell. A unit name with a quote breaks it, and anyone who can edit a config could make it run other commands. Pass the arguments as an array, with no shell. 2. Units run one at a time. Starting all of them at once with Promise.all could cut the nightly run from about two hours to minutes.
Both of those sound right. The last time something sounded right to me, I approved it.
Copilot Chat flagged a shell injection risk and a speed idea in the scheduler. What should Renata do?
A. Take the security fix only and leave the speed idea out of this ticket.
B. Ask Copilot to double check its two suggestions and follow its answer.
C. Take the fix with a test for the quote and measure the parallel run first.
D. Take both changes now that Copilot found them and every test passes.

The fix passes the arguments as an array, and a new test with Larkin's passes. Elena's script had built the same kind of string since 2016, and nobody had ever named a unit with a quote in it. Then they try all forty units at once in staging. The database replica runs out of connections in nine minutes. Four at a time takes thirty four minutes, down from two hours, and the replica stays calm. Ken reads the change and asks for the usual security scan anyway. Copilot found one. That doesn't mean there's only one.

That's how I'd chart it. Copilot Chat can find common vulnerabilities and suggest fixes, like not building commands from strings. GitHub says not to rely on it for a full security analysis, so keep code scanning. A performance suggestion is a change to measure. Faster in one place can overload another.
At ten Devin brought her the numbers slide. He'd volunteered for it, which he'd never done for a slide in eight years.
Board slide 3, Devin's draft. Copilot at Halcyon, last 28 days. 23,400 lines from Copilot suggestions added to our code. About two engineers' worth of work, every month
The first line is straight from GitHub's report. The second one is my math. I'm asking before I send it.
Devin's board slide counts Copilot lines and turns them into engineers' worth of work. What should Priya say?
A. Send the slide as it is, with the lines figure from GitHub's own report.
B. Lead with active users and merge times, with lines marked directional.
C. Keep the lines figure, drop the engineers line and add a method footnote.
D. Swap in the 31 percent acceptance rate as the measure of code quality.

They rebuild it together. Around forty six daily active users on a weekday, sixty one weekly. Agent mode up every week since November. Acceptance rate 31 percent. Median time to merge on Lumen down from twenty one hours, when Joyce counted in October, to seventeen. Lines added go at the bottom, marked directional. Then thirty eight answers from a short survey Nora ran, in people's own words. Devin reads the new version slowly. The lines number has the date bug in it. It has everything in it. That's why it's at the bottom.

That's what I'd want on my shift. Usage metrics show adoption, engagement, acceptance, lines of code, and pull request flow. GitHub says to read them together, with developer feedback. Lines are a directional view of output, not value, and acceptance shows trust, not correctness.
At 11:30 Renata opened her first big pull request: replace run_forecasts.pl with scheduler.ts. Thirty one files.
She'd already written three paragraphs in the description. Why the script was going. What she'd tested, and what she hadn't. The paused units rule, and that Elena had written it.
Then she noticed the Copilot icon in the header of the box, and the word Summary under it.
Do I use that? Mine took an hour. That would take a second.
Renata wrote three paragraphs in her PR description herself, and Copilot offers a Summary. What should she do?
A. Generate the summary on a blank box, then add her own notes back in.
B. Generate it now and post Copilot's summary in place of her paragraphs.
C. Have Copilot fold her three paragraphs, notes and all, into its summary.
D. Leave her own three paragraphs as the whole description for reviewers.

She cuts her paragraphs into a scratch file and clicks Summary on the empty box. It lists the changes well: the new scheduler, the config reader, the tests, four units at a time. One line says no behavior changes. That's wrong. The quoting changed, and so did the timing. She fixes the line, then pastes her three paragraphs under it. Anders reviews it that afternoon because he wants to. Who wrote the part about paused units? Me. Good. Copilot wouldn't have known it mattered.

That's the one I'd sign. On GitHub, the Copilot icon in a pull request's description or comment box offers Summary. Copilot doesn't take existing description text into account, so start blank. Then review what it wrote and add what only the author knows: why, how it was tested, and what to watch.
At one Renata showed her something else, a little shyly.

It was a dashboard for the retro: adoption by team, hours saved, a chart that climbed to the right. She'd tried GitHub Spark first, because a post from last year said it could build a whole app from one sentence. GitHub's page said Spark had stopped taking new apps in August. So she'd built it in VS Code with agent mode, in one evening.
The numbers were sample data. She'd had Copilot make them up, on purpose, so she could build the charts before the real report came.
Could it go in Thursday's deck? The numbers are probably close.
Renata's agent mode dashboard runs on sample numbers Copilot made up. How should it be used?
A. Put it in Thursday's board deck and keep the sample numbers as they are.
B. Show it at the retro as a design and give the board measured numbers only.
C. Use it Thursday with a small sample data note in the corner of each chart.
D. Tell her to pause side projects and wait until the rollout is finished.

It's a good design. It isn't evidence. The numbers are made up, and the board would read them as ours. Renata shows it at the retro with SAMPLE DATA across the top in red, and three people ask her to wire it to the real report in January. She writes that down. Then she crosses out hours saved on her own copy. Nobody had measured that.

That's how I'd chart it. A prototype with sample data shows what something could look like. Presenting made up numbers as results misleads people, which is why transparency and accountability matter. Generated data is for building and testing. Report what you measured.
The retro was at three in the big room, with Kraków on the screen. Priya had drawn three columns on the whiteboard: kept, changed, still wrong.
Devin put the first sticky note up, under changed: the date bug, in his own handwriting.
Ken's item was licenses. The public code policy had been on Block since October, and he wanted the retro to say what that did and didn't cover.
For the auditors, and for Thursday. Can I write that Copilot hasn't put anyone else's licensed code into Lumen?
A. Write only that the policy is set to Block and leave the rest to Ken.
B. Yes, the Block policy stops matching code everywhere Copilot runs.
C. Ask GitHub to confirm in writing that nothing in Lumen matches public code.
D. Write the setting and where it applies, with license checks still on us.

Nora writes it the way Ken says it. The policy setting and the date it last changed, from the audit log. Block covers suggestions in the editors. It doesn't cover the CLI, and the cloud agent can still write matching code, which it shows in its session logs. GitHub doesn't claim ownership of suggestions, so checking the licenses of what Halcyon ships is Halcyon's job, filter or no filter. That's a sentence I'd sign. Then sign it. He does.

That's what I'd want on my shift. The public code policy blocks matching suggestions in IDEs, but not every surface applies it, and the CLI and cloud agent can still produce matches. GitHub doesn't claim ownership of suggestions. Whether one can be owned depends on things like local law. Licensing what ships stays your job.
Thursday at ten the board met in the room with the long table. Elena sat at the end. Joyce sat beside Priya, not in front of her.
The numbers slide was up, the version she and Devin had rebuilt, with lines at the bottom.

Priya knew what a whole answer had in it. The date bug. The empty staging database in October. The seed rows her own July runbook had let through to Copilot. And numbers that could show people using Copilot, and couldn't show why anything had changed.
Elena folded her hands on the table. Priya. Was it worth it? Yes or no first.
In front of the board, how should Priya sum up the rollout?
A. Hand the answer to Joyce as the sponsor and let her speak to the board.
B. Say it's too early to tell and ask the board to wait for a full quarter.
C. Say yes so far, then lay out what broke and what still isn't known.
D. Yes, then lead with the strongest number and keep the incidents for questions.

Yes, so far. Then the rest, in order. What the seats cost. What broke, by date, and what changed after each one. What the numbers show, and what they can't: whether anything got faster because of Copilot, or because it was December. A board member asks how the seed rows got past everyone. My runbook. From July. I copied a line I should have checked. Elena writes something down. Afterward, in the hall, she stops Priya. That's the first slide about AI I've believed all year.

That's the one I'd sign. Responsible use includes reporting honestly: benefits, costs, harms, and limits. Transparency and accountability, two of the responsible AI principles GitHub follows, mean saying what went wrong and what changed, and not claiming more than the evidence shows.
Friday at 7:50 Elena wrote to all of engineering.

An email from Elena Vasquez. Subject: Next quarter. Team, The board said yes. Thank you. Next quarter I want Copilot approving the small pull requests on its own, so nobody waits a day for a review on a two line change. Elena
By 9:20 they were at Priya's desk. Anders, Ken, Devin with coffee, and Tomasz on Devin's laptop, where it was after five in Kraków. Joyce's office was twenty feet away. Nobody had gone there.
So, Anders said. What do we tell her?
A. Drop required reviews on small PRs, and let Copilot comment on them.
B. Tell her Copilot can't approve pull requests under any setting.
C. Keep people approving Lumen and pilot Copilot approvals on docs only.
D. Turn on Copilot approvals in every repository and let them count for merges.

We tell her what it can do today and where we'd let it, Priya says. Ken, read us the page. Ken reads GitHub's page aloud. By default Copilot leaves a Comment review, and its approval assessment doesn't count. Approvals that count are a public preview, off by default, and a repository can limit them to pull requests where every changed file matches its globs. So the reply proposes two things. Copilot reviews every pull request automatically, starting Monday. In the handbook repository, Copilot approvals count when every changed file is Markdown. Lumen keeps a person's name on every approval. Priya sends it under her name. Nobody suggests it should go under Joyce's.

That's how I'd chart it. By default Copilot code review leaves a Comment review, which doesn't count toward required approvals. Copilot approvals are in public preview and off by default. Admins can let them count toward merge requirements, limited by file paths. Keep human approval where the risk is real.
Elena answered at 2:10, to Priya, with everyone copied. Fine. People approve Lumen. Show me the handbook pilot in March.
She'd made most of the week's calls the way she'd want to explain them in March. She noticed she wasn't dreading March.

Sunday was dinner in Aurora, the last one before Christmas. Asha brought the cake from Havana Street and said it was worse than last year. Priya told them about the board, and about Friday at her desk.
Her father waited until the plates were stacked. Show me the thing.
In thirty years he hadn't asked to see her work. Not once. She went out to the car for her laptop.
He pulled his chair around to her side and put on his reading glasses, the drugstore pair he kept in his shirt pocket and claimed were Asha's. Asha stayed at her end of the table with her tea.

Priya opened the forecast code. There was a small fix she'd been meaning to make, a log line that printed the wrong unit name. She asked Copilot for it, read the answer, changed one line it got wrong, and ran the tests. Forty seconds, maybe a minute.
Raj had barely looked at the screen. He'd been watching her hands, which didn't touch the keys until she'd read to the end.
He put the glasses back in his pocket and said it to Asha, not to her. She reads it first. Then he carried the plates to the sink. He never let anybody dry.
Asha walked her out. It was cold enough that their breath showed under the porch light, and Asha had Raj's old cardigan on over her own sweater.
The first week, you sounded like a new grad on nights. Like nobody'd asked for you.
Friday morning, with Elena's email. Whose desk did they go to?

Priya started to answer and couldn't. Nobody had told them. Not Joyce, not Elena. Elena's email in October had put her name on the rollout. It couldn't make anybody bring her anything. Every week she'd done the next thing and asked somebody to check it, and every week somebody had.

Nobody hands you charge, Asha said. You take report. You do the next thing. And one night you look up and they're bringing you things. She hugged her and went back in before Priya could say anything, because it was nine degrees out and she'd said what she came out to say.
At the light on Colfax and Peoria, Priya called her anyway. She didn't have a question.
Asha answered before the second ring. You home?
Not yet. I'm calling to give report.
Everything that broke this quarter is written down, with what we changed after. What I still don't know is a list, and it's long. And Friday they came to my desk.
The light went green. That's a good report, Asha said. Text me when you're home. I'm not going to bed till you do.
